paraphrase: Whatever various figurative talk of 'self' and 'dharmas' goes on, it goes on with reference to the transformation of consciousness; and that transformation is of three kinds.

original.text: ātmadharmopacāro hi vividho yaḥ pravartate / vijñānapariṇāme 'sau pariṇāmaḥ sa ca tridhā

paraphrase: The mental factors are listed: the five universal (contact etc.); the five particular (desire-to-act, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom); eleven wholesome (faith, shame, embarrassment, the three roots non-greed etc., vigour, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, non-harming); the six afflictions (greed, aversion, delusion, conceit, views, doubt); the secondary afflictions (anger, enmity, concealment, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, dishonesty, pride, harmfulness, shamelessness, lack of embarrassment, torpor, agitation, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, non-awareness); and four that may go either way (regret, sleep, initial and sustained thought).

paraphrase: The five sense-consciousnesses arise in the root consciousness according to their conditions, together or not, like waves on water. Mind-consciousness arises always, except in the state of the non-perceiving gods, in the two mindless attainments, in deep sleep and in fainting.

original.text: pañcānāṃ mūlavijñāne yathāpratyayamudbhavaḥ / vijñānānāṃ saha na vā taraṅgāṇāṃ yathā jale

notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local DCS e-text of the Viṃśatikākārikā (22 verses).

notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local DCS e-text of the Viṃśatikākārikā (22 verses).

paraphrase: If you accept that, through beings' actions, elements arise in hell and transform, why not accept that consciousness transforms? You imagine the imprint of action in one place and its fruit in another; what reason is there not to accept the fruit where the imprint is?

original.text: karmaṇo vāsanānyatra phalamanyatra kalpyate / tatraiva neṣyate yatra vāsanā kiṃ nu kāraṇam

paraphrase: The Buddha taught the existence of the sense-fields (form etc.) with a particular intention for people to be trained, just as he spoke of beings of spontaneous birth; cognition arises from its own seed with the appearance of an object, and he called seed and appearance its two fields. Taught in this way, one enters the selflessness of persons; taught otherwise (as cognition-only), one enters the selflessness of dharmas — with respect to an imagined self (of dharmas).

original.text: rūpādyāyatanāstitvaṃ tadvineyajanaṃ prati / abhiprāyavaśāduktamupapādukasattvavat

original.text: na tadekaṃ na cānekaṃ viṣayaḥ paramāṇuśaḥ / na ca te saṃhatā yasmātparamāṇurna sidhyati

original.text: uktaṃ yathā tadābhāsā vijñaptiḥ smaraṇaṃ tataḥ / svapnadṛgviṣayābhāvaṃ nāprabuddho 'vagacchati

paraphrase: I have composed this proof of cognition-only according to my ability; in all its aspects it is inconceivable, the domain of the buddhas.

original.text: vijñaptimātratāsiddhiḥ svaśaktisadṛśī mayā / kṛteyaṃ sarvathā sā tu na cintyā buddhagocaraḥ

paraphrase: The imagined, the dependent and the perfected are the three natures, the deep object of the wise. What appears is the dependent, because it occurs in dependence on conditions; how it appears is the imagined, because it is mere imagination; the perfected is the constant non-existence of the appearing thing in the way it appears, because it is never otherwise.

original.text: kalpitaḥ paratantraśca pariniṣpanna eva ca / trayaḥ svabhāvā dhīrāṇāṃ gambhīrajñeyamiṣyate // yat khyāti paratantro 'sau yathā khyāti sa kalpitaḥ / pratyayādhīnavṛttitvāt kalpanāmātrabhāvataḥ

notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated.

paraphrase: Mind is twofold as cause and effect: the consciousness called ālaya, and the operative consciousness, sevenfold. The first is called 'mind' (citta) because it is accumulated (cita) with the seeds of defilement and imprints; the second because it occurs with variegated (citra) images. Unreal imagination is threefold: maturational (the root consciousness), causal, and appearing (the operative consciousness, seen, seer and seeing).
notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated.

paraphrase: The imagined is both existent and non-existent, since it is grasped as existent and is utterly non-existent; the dependent is both, since it exists as error and does not exist as it appears; the perfected is both, since it exists as non-duality and is the non-existence of duality.
notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated.

paraphrase: The three natures are taught in an order for the sake of convention and of entry: first one enters the dependent as the absence of duality; then one enters it as mere imagination, non-existent duality; then one enters the perfected, the being of the absence of duality — which is therefore said both to exist and not to exist.
notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated.

paraphrase: As a magical illusion produced by the power of a spell appears as an elephant — only the shape is there, the elephant not at all — so the imagined nature is the elephant, the dependent its shape, and the absence of the elephant there is the perfected. Unreal imagination appears from the root mind as duality; the duality does not exist at all; there is only the shape. The root consciousness is like the spell, suchness like the wood, imagination like the elephant's shape, duality like the elephant.

original.text: māyākṛtaṃ mantravaśāt khyāti hastyātmanā yathā / ākāramātraṃ tatrāsti hastī nāsti tu sarvathā

paraphrase: At the penetration of the truth of things, the three characteristics are simultaneously understood, abandoned and attained: understanding is non-apprehension, abandonment is non-appearance, attainment — which is also direct realization — is the apprehension without an image; by not apprehending duality the dual appearance vanishes, and with it the perfected, the absence of duality, is reached — just as in a magic show the non-apprehension of the elephant, the vanishing of its shape and the apprehension of the wood happen at once.
notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated.

paraphrase: Liberation comes without effort through seeing that cognition obstructs the contrary cognition, through seeing the futility (of the object) by understanding, and through the continuation of the three knowledges.
notes: Verse numbering and wording checked against the local GRETIL Devanāgarī e-text (Anacker ed.), transliterated. The verse is compressed; paraphrase follows its three ablatives closely and is to be checked by extraction.

paraphrase: Through the apprehension of mind-only comes the non-apprehension of knowable objects; through the non-apprehension of knowable objects comes the non-apprehension of mind; through the non-apprehension of both comes the apprehension of the dharmadhātu; through the apprehension of the dharmadhātu comes mastery; and having mastery and accomplishing his own and others' aims, the wise one attains unsurpassed awakening, whose nature is the three bodies.

paraphrase: Emptiness is explained by its characteristic, synonyms, their meaning, divisions and proof. Its synonyms are suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate and the dharmadhātu — meaning unchanging, non-erroneous, cessation of signs, object of the noble ones' cognition, and cause of the noble qualities.

If it were defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated; if it were pure, effort would be fruitless. It is neither defiled nor undefiled, neither pure nor impure, because the mind is luminous and the defilements are adventitious.

paraphrase: Stability of mind for success in all aims arises from abandoning five faults and applying eight formations. The five faults are laziness, forgetting the instruction, sinking and agitation, non-application and (over-)application. The eight formations are the basis (desire-to-act), the based (effort), its cause (faith), its fruit (pliancy), non-forgetting of the object (mindfulness), noticing sinking and agitation (awareness), the application to remove them (intention), and calm flow when they have ceased (equanimity).

paraphrase: Having amassed the accumulations of merit and knowledge, the bodhisattva, well settled in reflection on the teachings, understands that objects arise from mental speech; knowing objects as mere speech he rests in mind-only that appears as them; then the dharmadhātu becomes directly perceived, free of the characteristic of duality. Understanding by insight that nothing exists apart from mind, he then understands the non-existence of mind itself; understanding the non-existence of both, the wise one rests in the dharmadhātu, which is not that (duality).

paraphrase: Mirror-like wisdom is unmoving, and the three other wisdoms depend on it: equality, discernment and accomplishment of what is to be done. Mirror-like wisdom is without 'mine', unbounded, always present, unconfused about all knowables yet never facing them; equality-wisdom sees beings as equal and abides in non-abiding peace; discerning wisdom is unobstructed toward all knowables, like a treasury of dhāraṇīs and concentrations, and rains the Dharma; the wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done acts for all beings through countless emanations.

paraphrase: The path of calm is the gathering of the teachings' names, the path of insight the investigation of their meanings, and their union the joined path. One should lift the sunken mind and calm the agitated one; when calm is reached, let it be; then: fix the mind on the object and not let it stray; notice distraction quickly and bring it back; withdraw the mind inward ever more; delight it in concentration by seeing its qualities; quell displeasure by seeing the fault of distraction; quell covetousness, grief and the like as they arise; then the mind flows by itself with effort; and by practice it flows without effort.

paraphrase: Then the bodhisattva in concentration no longer sees objects apart from mental speech (heat); he strives firmly to increase the light of the teaching (peak); by its increase he abides in mind-only and sees all objects as appearances in mind, and the distraction of the grasped is abandoned (patience); only the distraction of the grasper remains, and he quickly touches the immediate concentration (supreme mundane quality); after it the distraction of the grasper also ends. These are heat and the others in order. Then he gains supramundane, unsurpassed, non-conceptual, stainless knowledge free from the grasping of duality.

paraphrase: All that is to be known is summed up in two: dharmas and their nature (dharmatā). Dharmas are saṃsāra, characterized by the appearance of duality and of verbal designation, arising from unreal imagination; dharmatā is nirvāṇa, characterized by suchness without the division of grasped and grasper, of object of expression and expression.

paraphrase: Entry into non-conceptual wisdom proceeds through the non-apprehension of objects on the basis of apprehending mind-only, and the non-apprehension of mind-only on the basis of not apprehending objects; the transformation of the basis is explained under ten headings (nature, substance, persons, distinctive features, requirements, basis, attention, application, drawbacks of its absence and benefits).

paraphrase: The lineage (gotra) of a disciple is the seed of the qualities of liberation already present; one who has it can attain nirvāṇa given the right conditions — human birth, a central land, intact faculties, faith, the appearance of a buddha, the teaching and a spiritual friend.

These are accomplished by six powers — hearing, reflection, mindfulness, awareness, vigour and familiarity — and accompanied by four attentions: forced, interrupted, uninterrupted and spontaneous.

paraphrase: The Yogācārabhūmi is summed up in seventeen stages: that associated with the five sense-consciousnesses; the mental stage; those with initial and sustained thought, with sustained thought only, and with neither; the concentrated and the unconcentrated; with mind and without mind; those made of hearing, reflection and cultivation; the stages of the disciples, the solitary buddhas and the bodhisattvas; and those with and without remainder.

paraphrase: The store-consciousness must be accepted: without it the appropriation of a new body, the simultaneous functioning of several consciousnesses, the clarity of mental cognition, the planting of seeds, the karmic process, bodily experience, the mindless attainments and death could not be explained (the eight proofs).
notes: The eight headings are recalled (the Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya and Tsongkhapa's 'Mind and Basis' reproduce them); to be checked.

paraphrase: The path is fivefold: the path of accumulation, the path of preparation, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation and the path of completion. The path of seeing consists of sixteen moments of mind — eight acceptances and eight knowledges regarding the four truths.

paraphrase: The consciousness-aggregate is mind, mentation and consciousness; mind (citta) is the store-consciousness, perfumed by the imprints of aggregates, elements and bases, holding all seeds, also called maturation-consciousness and appropriating consciousness; mentation (manas) is what always takes the store-consciousness as 'I', associated with four afflictions: self-view, self-love, the conceit 'I am' and ignorance.

paraphrase: The basis of the knowable is the store-consciousness, called ālaya because all defiled dharmas are stored in it as effects and it in them as cause, and 'appropriating consciousness' (ādāna) because it appropriates the body; it is proved by scripture and reasoning, and its seeds are momentary, simultaneous with their fruit, continuous, determinate, dependent on conditions and productive of their own fruit.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese. The six characteristics of seeds are recalled.

paraphrase: The characteristic of the knowable is the three natures: the dependent nature is cognition-only arising from the seeds of the store; the imagined is its appearing as objects though there are none; the perfected is the dependent's complete absence of the imagined object. The dependent partakes of both defilement and purification.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese.

paraphrase: Entry into the characteristic of the knowable is entry into cognition-only: hearing the Mahāyāna teaching, the bodhisattva at the stage of practice by resolve first understands that names, meanings, own-natures and particulars are mere designations (four investigations and four exact knowledges), then that objects are cognition-only, then that even cognition-only does not appear, and enters the path of seeing.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese.

paraphrase: Higher wisdom is non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpa-jñāna): preparatory, fundamental and subsequently obtained; it is not mere absence of thought, nor like the unconsciousness of sleep or of the mindless attainments, but a cognition that does not construct its object.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese.

paraphrase: The fruit as abandonment is the transformation of the basis — the dependent nature turned from its defiled to its purified side — and non-abiding nirvāṇa, which abides neither in saṃsāra nor in (a quiescent) nirvāṇa.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese.

paraphrase: The fruit as wisdom is the three bodies of a buddha: the essential body (dharmakāya), the enjoyment body and the transformation body, the first being the support of the other two.
notes: Chapter-level reference (Lamotte's chapter division); no Sanskrit original; paraphrase from memory of the Tibetan/Chinese.

paraphrase: The appropriating consciousness (ādāna-vijñāna) is deep and subtle; with all its seeds it flows like a torrent; I have not taught it to the childish, lest they imagine it to be a self.
speaker: the Buddha
notes: Chapter-level ref following Lamotte's ten-chapter division; paraphrase from memory; U39 owns the source. The Sanskrit verse is quoted in Sthiramati's Triṃśikābhāṣya and the Mahāyānasaṃgraha (SNS 5.7 in Lamotte's numbering, recalled).

paraphrase: Dharmas have three characteristics: the imagined characteristic (names and conventions positing own-being and particulars), the dependent characteristic (their dependent origination) and the perfected characteristic (their suchness) — illustrated by the eye-disease (imagined), the hairs seen by it (dependent) and the undistorted object seen by clear eyes (perfected).
speaker: the Buddha
notes: Chapter-level ref following Lamotte's ten-chapter division; paraphrase from memory; U39 owns the source. The simile's mapping is recalled; to be checked.

paraphrase: When I taught that all dharmas are without own-nature, unborn, unceasing, primordially at peace and naturally in nirvāṇa, I intended three kinds of naturelessness: of characteristic, of arising and ultimate. The first turning of the wheel (the four truths, at Vārāṇasī) and the second (the naturelessness of dharmas) were surpassable and of provisional meaning; this third, well-distinguished turning is unsurpassable and of definitive meaning.

paraphrase: The image that is the object of concentration is not different from the mind, because consciousness is distinguished by cognition-only of its object; the mind sees the mind; the practice of calm and insight is explained, with their objects (images with and without conceptualization, the limit of things, the accomplishment of the aim).

paraphrase: As waves rise on the ocean stirred by the wind, so the operative consciousnesses arise from the store-consciousness stirred by the wind of objects; they are neither different nor non-different from it, as the waves from the ocean.

paraphrase: There are five lineages of realization: of the disciples' vehicle, of the solitary buddhas' vehicle, of the Tathāgata-vehicle, the undetermined, and the fifth, without lineage.

paraphrase: Mounting to mind-only, one should not imagine an external object; abiding in the object that is suchness, one should pass beyond mind-only; passing beyond mind-only, one should pass beyond the imageless; the yogin abiding in the imageless sees the Mahāyāna. The effortless state is peaceful, purified by vows; the supreme selfless wisdom is not seen in the imageless.

paraphrase: Kamalaśīla explains the Laṅkāvatāra's verses as stages of meditation: the yogin first analyses form as nothing apart from mind, then examines mind itself and finds it without own-nature, then abandons even the image of non-duality, and abides in the imageless wisdom that sees the Mahāyāna.
notes: Section-level ref in the first Bhāvanākrama (local e-text asian_classics); paraphrase condensed.

paraphrase: The Thirty Verses were composed to teach the selflessness of persons and of dharmas to those who misunderstand or do not understand them; teaching them serves to abandon the afflictive and the cognitive obscurations, since the afflictions arise from self-view and the cognitive obscuration is removed by knowing the selflessness of dharmas.

paraphrase: Bodily and verbal action are not real entities; action is volition, which leaves an impression in the mental series; since mind is interrupted in the mindless attainments, a maturation-consciousness holding the seeds must continue through them, and this is the ālaya-vijñāna.
notes: Section-level summary from memory of Lamotte's translation.

paraphrase: Against the objection that the Mahāyāna sūtras are not the Buddha's word, Vasubandhu argues that much of the Buddha's teaching has been lost, that the Mahāyāna sūtras accord with the Dharma's marks and lead to awakening, and that the disciples' own canon contains passages presupposing them.
notes: Chapter-level (ch. 4) and content recalled; to be checked.

paraphrase: Consciousness is the cognition of objects; it is also called mind because it is variegated and because it is accumulated with seeds; in the principal sense it is the store-consciousness, and mentation (manas) is that which takes it as its object and is always accompanied by the afflictions of self.
notes: Section on the consciousness aggregate; paraphrase from memory.

paraphrase: The bodhisattva vow is to be taken from a teacher who keeps and understands it and is competent; the four root downfalls (as in the Bodhisattvabhūmi) and forty-six lesser faults are to be avoided; a downfall committed with strong affliction destroys the vow, which may be taken again; lesser faults are confessed.
notes: Summary of the whole text; the count of forty-six lesser faults is the Tibetan commentarial count.

paraphrase: Every cognition has four parts: the seen part (image), the seeing part, the self-witnessing part and the witnessing of the self-witnessing part (Dharmapāla's view, against those who admit one, two or three parts); seeds are both originally present and newly perfumed.
notes: Fascicle (juan)-level reference, from memory; to be checked against T1585.

paraphrase: Self and dharmas are refuted: they are mere designations based on the transformations of consciousness; the self of the non-Buddhists and the real dharmas of the Hīnayāna schools are both rejected.
notes: Fascicle (juan)-level reference, from memory; to be checked against T1585.

paraphrase: The path to cognition-only has five stages: accumulation, preparation (with the four stages heat, peak, patience and supreme mundane quality, in which the grasped and then the grasper are seen as empty), penetration (the path of seeing), cultivation (through the ten grounds), and final attainment.
notes: Fascicle (juan)-level reference, from memory; to be checked against T1585. The five-stage account spans juan 9–10.

paraphrase: At buddhahood the eight consciousnesses are transformed into four wisdoms: the eighth into great mirror-wisdom, the seventh into equality-wisdom, the sixth into discerning wisdom, the five senses into the wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done; the sixth and seventh begin to turn at the path of seeing, the eighth and the five senses only at buddhahood.
notes: Fascicle (juan)-level reference, from memory; to be checked against T1585.
